sections.body_en:
1

I thank Hashem for having granted me the merit to learn Torah and to teach it, and now He has granted me the merit to complete the writing of the laws of Shevi'it and the main laws of the Yovel. In these mitzvot all the values of the Torah are included together, in keeping with the foundation of the faith of Israel: to reveal the Divine light in all the layers and spheres of the world together.

The mitzva depends on the Jewish people as a whole, for by Torah law one is obligated in Shevi'it and Yovel only when all Israel dwell in their Land as they should (below 5:1). And this mitzva also depends on each and every individual, for in practice it is fulfilled by the individuals who let their fields lie fallow, free the slaves and return the lands in the Yovel. Its fulfilment depends on the Land of Israel, for only in the Land of Israel is there a mitzva to rest in Shevi'it and to hold the Yovel (below 5:8). And it depends on time in two senses: first, only when all Israel dwell in their Land are they obligated in Shevi'it, and when part of Israel is in exile the obligation is rabbinic. Second, when Israel dwell in their Land, they are commanded to count years and to rest in the seventh year and to hold the Yovel in the fiftieth year (below 5:1-7). Thus the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel bind together soul and body, spirit and action, for in resting in the seventh year there is an aspect of elevation and holiness like Shabbat. At the same time the fulfilment of Shevi'it and Yovel goes down to the depths of the earth: to declare the produce ownerless and to release debts in Shevi'it, and to free slaves and return fields in the Yovel. These mitzvot also join miracle and nature, for the reality of an entire people resting from the work of its fields for a whole year seems impossible; but in practice, by virtue of Shevi'it, blessing spreads over all six years, and this blessing does not come by way of miracle but by way of nature (below 1:7-8; 7:10). This is the meaning of the Torah's emphasis that these mitzvot were said to Moshe at Sinai: because they include within them all the values of the Torah. Therefore it is said (Vayikra 25:1-2): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe on Mount Sinai, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord." And the Sages added (Sifra there) that from this we learn that just as the general rules and fine details of the mitzva of Shevi'it were said to Moshe at Sinai, so too all the mitzvot, their general rules and fine details, are from Sinai. Thus from the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel, which embrace all the values together and reveal the Divine light in all spheres, we learn that this is the concern of the whole Torah and of all the mitzvot that were given to us at Sinai.

Apparently, because the mitzva of Shevi'it binds together many spheres, the debates about its fulfilment also extend to many spheres: to questions of the community and the individual, to the relationship between the various circles, to the relationship between practical consideration and reliance on miracles, and to the question of exile and redemption. Since this subject is so complex, one may say that from the way this subject is studied, a straight path can be paved for the study of the whole Torah.

We have merited that Hashem sent us in the recent generations the great seer, greatest of the great, most pious of the pious, Maran Rav Avraham Yitzḥak Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l, the rabbi of the Land of Israel, to pave for us the way to the fulfilment of the mitzva of Shevi'it and to the fulfilment of the whole Torah. There was none like him, great in Torah, in the recent generations, and his greatness was in all spheres: Scripture and Gemara, analysis and halakha, aggada and kabbala, Ḥasidut and research, the general rules and the details. At times the richness of his wisdom was a hindrance to him, for he understood all the views in depth and always wanted to satisfy all of them. And even when things seemed contradictory, in the depth, greatness and breadth of his thought he saw how they complement one another. But in practice, when the different ideas came to a practical contradiction, he was pained and suffered from the need to choose and decide for one side. And nevertheless, by the power of the greatness of his Torah he decided the halakha and paved the straight and complete path in the Torah. So too in the subjects of Shevi'it: on the one hand he was greatly pained by the exile of the nation and the deficiency in the building of the Land, and he greatly longed to fulfil the mitzvot as they will be obligatory in the future, for he saw the hidden light in them. And on the other hand, he decided that in the present situation it is necessary to use the 'heter mekhira' (the sale permit) for the sake of the community and the individual, and for the sake of fulfilling the mitzva of settling the Land and bringing the redemption closer. Therefore at times the superficial learner finds seeming contradictions in his words; but they stem from the greatness and breadth of his mind, which contained all the ideas, even the contradictory ones, and at times he explains from this side and at times from that side. Therefore he also understood his opponents, and even loved them, although he suffered bitterness from them. In this book I have tried to follow his path, according to what he ruled for the Jewish people as a whole. But unlike his extraordinary piety, in which he wanted from the outset to satisfy everyone and also understood those who disagreed with him and the good motive behind their errors, I have followed the ordinary path of halakha according to the decisive majority of the poskim.

2

The magnitude of the privilege that has fallen to my lot cannot be estimated: that the students of the yeshiva, together with the residents of the community of Har Bracha, are full partners in this book, as in the ones before it. From the beginning of the winter term until Rosh Ḥodesh Tammuz 5775 I was occupied with the study of the laws of Shevi'it, and from time to time in the daily shiur in the yeshiva I shared with the students the questions and explanations that had newly arisen; and in the months of Iyar and Sivan the daily shiur in the yeshiva was devoted to studying the laws of Shevi'it in order. Naturally, since most of my thoughts were occupied with the mitzva of Shevi'it, the Shabbat derashot and the shiurim for the residents of the community also dealt with these subjects. And from time to time, when I merited to explain an obscure subject, I could not help announcing it publicly in the Friday night derasha, and the next day at noon I would explain the subject in the large shiur for women, and even more broadly towards the end of Shabbat in the large derasha for men. I also shared with my listeners the story of the history of Shevi'it and of the renewed settlement in the Land, and my thoughts and the storm in my heart about the disputes surrounding the 'heter mekhira' and the settlement of the Land, and their public implications. On all the subjects discussed I merited to hear questions and answers, comments and insights. And since the make-up of those who hear the shiurim is varied, the questions, comments and insights come from all spheres: from the kitchen and from the beit midrash, from the markets and from the extended families, from experts, men and women, in history, economics and society. Also the listeners who nodded their heads when things were well explained made their contribution. All of them are full partners in this book. "I have learned much from my teachers, and from my colleagues more than from my teachers, and from my students more than from all of them" (Ta'anit 7a).

Out of fulfilling the mitzva of settling the Land on the front line of settlement in the heart of the Shomron, this book on Shevi'it and Yovel grew and was written, and all of it is a prayer for the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the whole Land in its length and breadth, until we merit to fulfil the mitzvot of Shevi'it and Yovel as stated in the Torah, in the full force of their obligation and holiness. I will further mention our relative Nir Lavi, who planted vineyards around the community, and merited that through him the words of the prophet were fulfilled (Yirmiyahu 31:3-4): "Again I will build you and you shall be built, O virgin of Israel; again you shall adorn yourself with your timbrels and go forth in the dances of those who make merry. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Shomron; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit." In the course of this I also came into close contact with the practical laws for farmers in Shevi'it.

3

It is a great privilege for me to thank the close partners in studying the subjects: Rav Maor Kayam shlit"a, a ram in Yeshivat Har Bracha, who accompanies me throughout the study, and with his talent and diligence helps to clarify the subjects, rejoices in my explanations and new insights and at the same time criticises them strictly, so that everything comes out properly clarified. And thanks also to Rav Yair Weitz, who helped with proofreading and clarifying the subjects, and was especially meticulous on the subject of the borders and the years, from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun until our time. I also thank Maor Horowitz, who with speed and meticulousness helped to clarify the sources and with the work of content and language proofreading and preparing the book for print. Thanks also to Rav Uriel Shalmoni for the deep comments and the additional sources. And thanks too to Rav Dr. Boaz Huterer for his contribution in clarifying the subjects from a historical perspective. Thanks to Rav Yonadav Zar for the precise proofreading and the encouragement, and to R. Netanel Rosenstein for writing the index. And thanks too to my good and long-time friend, the comprehensive scholar, Rav Ze'ev Sultanovitch, who clarified the general subjects with me.

4

It is a very pleasant duty to mention with praise the books composed in the last generation that greatly helped us in studying the subjects. First and foremost the 'Machon Ha-Torah Ve-Ha-Aretz', which merited to publish a critical edition of the book of Maran Rav Kook zt"l, 'Shabbat Ha-Aretz', with the addition of all the sources from the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim. There is no other book on Shevi'it as detailed and rich in sources as it. The Torah scholars who are members of this institute also wrote the important book 'Ketif Shevi'it', in which they summarised all the laws and the professional guidance for farmers and gardeners. Special thanks to Rav Yehuda Amiḥai shlit"a, who in addition to heading the institute wrote excellent articles on the subjects of Shevi'it and the mitzvot dependent on the Land, and they are scattered in the books of 'Machon Ha-Torah Ve-Ha-Aretz' and its journals. Of course I was also helped by the book of the institute's president, Rav Yaakov Ariel shlit"a, 'Be-Ohalah Shel Torah', and by the important articles of his son, my friend from youth, Rav Azriel Ariel shlit"a. I will also mention my teacher and master Rav Shaul Yisraeli zt"l, by whose strength and encouragement this important institute was founded, and which continues his halakhic enterprise. I will also mention Rav Yehoshua Magnes shlit"a, who merited to publish the important introduction to 'Shabbat Ha-Aretz' of Maran the Rav, with important additions of explanations, comments and expansions. It is fitting also to mention the book of my friend Rav Yehuda Zoldan shlit"a, 'Malkhut Yehuda Ve-Yisrael'.

Throughout the study we were helped by the important book of my teacher and master, the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu zt"l, 'Ma'amar Mordekhai', which contains settled halakhot, as was his holy way, and many analyses. Many times I followed his path. I will also mention with praise two books: 'Mishpetei Eretz' of the 'Beit Midrash Gavoha Le-Halakha Be-Hityashvut Ha-Ḥakla'it', which is important, systematic and precise; and likewise the book 'Shevitat Ha-Sadeh' by Rav Shneur Revaḥ of the 'Institute for the Mitzvot Dependent on the Land', which summarises the subjects clearly and broadly.

On the matter of the heter mekhira, it is an obligation to mention with appreciation the comprehensive clarifications of the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Ovadia Yosef zt"l, which are brought in his important book Yabia Omer vol. 10 (YD 37-44). It is also fitting to mention the deep and clear book 'Likrat Shemita Mamlakhtit Bi-Medinat Yisrael' by my friend Rav Ze'ev Whitman shlit"a, who wrote it out of his breadth of mind and his familiarity with reality. I will also mention with thanks my friend Rav Yehoshua Ben Meir shlit"a, author of the book 'Ma Nokhal Ba-Shana Ha-Shevi'it – Heter Mekhira O Otzar Beit Din', in which he clarifies precisely the view of Maran Rav Kook and most of his followers, who held that the 'heter mekhira' is the right solution and not 'otzar beit din'; and in addition he went over the chapters of the book and made me wiser with his comments. I will also mention with praise the fine and well-clarified book of my friend Rav Yosef Tzvi Rimon shlit"a, 'Shemita – Halakha Mi-Mekorah', from which the learner gains a broad and comprehensive picture of all the subjects of shemita. I also thank my friend Rav Yehuda Brandes shlit"a for his illuminating comments; and likewise Rav Shlomo Ishon shlit"a for his comments on the matter of the release of debts.

5

Offerings of thanks to my father and teacher, Rav Zalman Barukh Melamed shlit"a, Rosh Yeshivat Beit El, and to my mother and teacher, from whom come all the foundations of my Torah and outlook. And special thanks to Inbal, my dear wife, who devotes all her strength to magnifying and glorifying the Torah, to the success of the study and to publishing the books for the benefit of the many. May it be His will that we merit to see all our sons and daughters, our grandsons and granddaughters, rising in Torah study and the fulfilment of mitzvot, establishing good and splendid families, and increasing truth, kindness and peace for ever.

I will further thank all those engaged in the holy work of building the yeshiva and printing the books: R. Yaakov Weinberger, director of the yeshiva; Keren Fogel, in charge of printing and distribution; Ḥaim Margolis, in charge of marketing; and those before them in the management of the yeshiva and the printing of the books, R. Yaakov Katz, R. Dudu Sa'ada and R. Yisrael Sa'adia. May it be the will of Hashem, blessed be He, to give all those who help and assist in the work understanding and strength to succeed in their work, and may they merit to establish splendid families, and may Hashem fulfil all the wishes of their hearts for the good.

Eliezer Melamed

Tammuz 5775
